extracted.intended_audience: government administrators, project teams and legal services personnel responsible for implementing PAJA mainstreaming in organs of state
extracted.subtask_description: Practical implementation guidance for mainstreaming the Promotion of Administrative Justice Act (PAJA) into government business processes, including roles, core principles, a five‑phase model, tools and self‑assessment checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi‑stakeholder project teams
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a need to have multi‑stakeholder teams. The PAJA cuts across all business units and therefore impacts on every administrator involved in the administrative decision‑making process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mainstreaming teams should consist of both legal services personnel as well as administrators involved in decision‑making. This ensures subject knowledge across legal and operational perspectives and that the teams reflect all business units affected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active and consistent management support
rubrics_metrics.description: Management support is vital in the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pilots that succeeded indicated consistent and active management involvement throughout the project. Management committees/teams need to drive the mainstreaming process, receive progress reports, approve changes to decision‑making procedures, and communicate objectives to secure organisational acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement of all administrators across business processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Engage all administrators involved in a business process from beginning to end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because administrative decision‑making can be staggered and different administrators can influence final decisions, all administrators who play any role in the decision process should be engaged in mainstreaming activities to ensure comprehensive alignment and avoid gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project champion / dedicated project team
rubrics_metrics.description: The need for a project champion or project team to drive and steer the PAJA mainstreaming project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'driver' ensures the project is initiated, momentum is maintained, progress is monitored and communication with stakeholders occurs. Nomination of a project champion/team is an early management action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senior Management responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Senior Management: nominate the Project Team; communicate with stakeholders about PAJA mainstreaming to get support and convey objectives; receive progress reports; approve changes to decision‑making procedures or related processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Senior management should actively endorse the initiative, keep governance oversight, and provide authority for amendments to institutional arrangements. Use management meeting agenda templates to structure initiation discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project Team responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Project Team: initiate the project; meet with administrators from respective business units; develop the project plan; monitor mainstreaming activities; offer support and unblock barriers; provide regular reports to management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The project team steers day‑to‑day implementation; it must clarify roles, set timeframes, and use provided implementation tools (e.g., project plan template, agenda templates). The team should meet regularly and use the self‑assessment tools at phase ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business unit administrators' responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrators of business units responsible for core business processes: conduct introductory training on PAJA mainstreaming; lead and guide business units through the phases; conduct practical working sessions with stakeholders; compile data from working sessions; report on progress; manage implementation of changes in partnership with respective personnel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrators should lead operational change, facilitate working sessions, collect evidence and report progress. They must work with legal services and the project team when implementing amended processes, forms and letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal services personnel responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal Services Personnel: participate in PAJA mainstreaming project teams; support implementation of mainstreaming changes; conduct training when needed; check and review amended decision‑making flows for PAJA compliance when necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal advisors should be consulted when determining whether decisions are administrative actions, and to ensure amended flows, procedures and templates comply with PAJA. Their role is both advisory and training/supportive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personnel involved in business processes responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Staff involved at any point in the business process: participate fully in all phases of the PAJA mainstreaming process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participation includes identifying administrative decisions, mapping decision‑making processes, analysing alignment to PAJA, identifying gaps, suggesting changes to close gaps, and implementing changed procedures, forms and letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core principle: Involvement of key role‑players
rubrics_metrics.description: Involvement of key role‑players wherever possible; involve the people doing the business processes being analysed in the mainstreaming process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This promotes ownership of changes, understanding of reasons and purpose, and builds capacity for continuous improvement. Ensure facilitators are present in working sessions and that affected staff are involved and heard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core principle: Communicate consistently
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication allows people to understand the purpose, builds awareness and supports buy‑in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communicate at all phases (initiation, analysis/amendment, implementation). Communicate with management (purpose/progress/outcomes) and staff (roles/expectations/process). Establish agreed methods and schedules for communication and documentation of meetings and decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core principle: Adopt a project management approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a planned, organised project‑based approach to mainstreaming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine activities and set time‑frames; identify priorities (e.g., two most important administrative decisions), set step timeframes with clear end dates; monitor and review progress consistently. Use provided implementation tools (agenda template, project plan template).

rubrics_metrics.name: Core principle: Build knowledge and understanding of PAJA across the department
rubrics_metrics.description: Constantly build administrators' knowledge about PAJA to enable participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use short presentations, enrol staff in PAJA training courses (PALAMA, Justice College), and use Information Sheets to introduce key concepts. Training should be ongoing and tailored to roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core principle: Identify opportunities for continuous improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Mainstreaming is an opportunity to highlight inefficiencies and improve business processes beyond PAJA compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where appropriate, streamline processes, improve communication flows, and use mainstreaming to enhance overall operational efficiency while ensuring PAJA compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five‑phase implementation model (overview)
rubrics_metrics.description: The PAJA mainstreaming model comprises five phases: Phase 1 — Establish shared objectives and commitment; Phase 2 — Identify and prioritise administrative decisions; Phase 3 — Analyse administrative decision‑making processes for PAJA compliance; Phase 4 — Amend decision‑making processes and tools; Phase 5 — Implement and monitor the PAJA mainstreaming implementation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each phase contains: phase purpose, key activities, information sheets, resources and implementation tools. Teams should read information sheets and use practical tools; perform self‑assessment at the end of each phase before progressing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase 1: Establish shared objectives and commitment (purpose & activities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Purpose: establish the building blocks for successful implementation (management support, buy‑in, communicating the process, establish project manager/team).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key activities: create management support and buy‑in (use agenda template); communicate information about PAJA mainstreaming (use PPT tool); establish a project team; develop a project plan (use project plan template). Remember the core implementation principles and roles/responsibilities. Use Implementation Tools 1–3 and Information Sheets 1–2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase 2: Identify and prioritise administrative decisions (purpose & activities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Purpose: create active participation and collaboration among administrators and legal services; build a common information base about which administrative decisions are PAJA administrative actions; ensure administrative decisions are lawful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key activities: check that administrative actions are envisaged by PAJA (Information Sheet 3); decide on key administrative decisions to be analysed; use Implementation Tool 4 (Identifying administrative decisions). Encourage consultation with legal advisors when in doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase 3: Analyse decision‑making processes for PAJA compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyse administrative decision‑making processes to determine alignment with PAJA and identify gaps requiring amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use practical working sessions to map decision flows, identify the administrators involved at each step, determine where PAJA requirements are not met, and compile the data for proposed changes. Use implementation tools and information sheets provided for detailed steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase 4: Amend decision‑making processes and tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Amend processes, procedures, forms, letters and tools to close gaps identified in analysis and to ensure PAJA compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manage implementation of changes in partnership with relevant personnel and legal services. Pilot amended procedures where feasible, provide training, and update documentation and templates. Monitor for unintended consequences and modify as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase 5: Implement and monitor the mainstreaming implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement amended decision‑making processes and monitor their effectiveness and compliance with PAJA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set monitoring indicators, collect progress data, review and refine processes, and ensure sustainability through continued training and integration into routine business practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase 1 self‑assessment progress indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Self‑assessment tool items to check progress before moving from Phase 1 to Phase 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Progress indicators include: (1) Management has nominated a project team; (2) Project team consists of legal services personnel and administrators; (3) Project team has met to discuss roles/responsibilities and develop a project plan; (4) Project team has met with management to discuss project purpose, objectives, process and time‑frames; (5) Project team has communicated information about the mainstreaming process to all affected stakeholders; (6) Support and buy‑in exists for the project. Use these as go/no‑go checks prior to Phase 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Elements that define an administrative action (Overview)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are six key elements that help establish whether a decision is an administrative action under PAJA; if a decision satisfies these elements it is considered an administrative action governed by PAJA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the six elements listed below as a checklist when determining whether a given administrative decision falls within PAJA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element 1 — It must be a decision (or failure to take a decision)
rubrics_metrics.description: An administrative action is a decision; or a failure to take a decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A failure to make a decision can have major negative effects and may therefore constitute an administrative action subject to PAJA. Treat refusals/omissions with same rigor as affirmative decisions when assessing coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element 2 — Of an administrative nature made in terms of an empowering provision
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions that administrators take as part of their job are administrative in nature and must be made in terms of an empowering provision (usually a statutory provision granting power).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The empowering provision ensures the decision is lawful and within the administrator's powers. If not made under an empowering provision, it may not qualify as a PAJA administrative action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element 3 — Not specifically excluded by PAJA
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision must not be specifically excluded by PAJA (e.g., high‑level policy decisions of the executive; making of legislation by Parliament/provincial legislature/municipal council; exercise of judicial functions by courts and some bodies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check statutory exclusions before treating a decision as an administrative action. Some categories of decisions are explicitly outside PAJA's scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element 4 — Made by an organ of state
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision must be made by an organ of state (departments at national/provincial/municipal level; functionaries/institutions exercising powers under legislation; private individuals/companies exercising public power).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the factual nature of the actor: private parties exercising public power may fall within PAJA. Verify institutional status when determining coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element 5 — Adversely affects rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision adversely affects the rights of someone or a group (negative effect, limits or removes rights, or decides someone does not have a right).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beneficial decisions generally are not administrative actions. Consider whether the decision imposes a detriment, limitation, or denial of rights or interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element 6 — Has direct external legal effect (legal effect, direct effect, external effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision must have legal effect (legally binding), direct effect (the final step that affects a member of the public), and external effect (affects someone outside the organ of state).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a decision forms part of several internal steps and only the last step affects the public, only the last step is the administrative action. Ensure the decision produces a legally binding external result to fall within this element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementation Tool 4: Steps to identify and prioritise administrative decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidelines: (1) List all administrative decisions made in your business unit; (2) Determine whether listed decisions are administrative actions (use the six elements); (3) Prioritise the administrative decisions to be analysed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Information Sheet 3 (Elements that define an administrative action) to assist determinations. Consult legal advisors where necessary. Prioritisation helps focus limited resources on the most important decisions for analysis and amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative team practices (Information Sheet 1 guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical steps to get collaboration and active involvement: have a clear goal; establish communication methods; decide on how senior management will be kept in the loop; define team member roles; appoint a facilitator for working sessions; establish monitoring and feedback processes; agree a common approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use meeting templates, define tasks and responsibilities, set regular meetings and documentation practices, and ensure the team agrees how to adapt the guide to local circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing change principles (Information Sheet 2 guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles to assist teams manage change: you cannot impose change; people need to understand purpose and intentions; create a simple plan of action with defined roles; develop an enabling environment (training, communications, aligned team meetings); celebrate achievements; communicate effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empower staff to co‑design responses; present the rationale for PAJA mainstreaming; break the plan into small achievable chunks; provide training and recognition to sustain motivation and overcome resistance.
